mainTopic: How a Jew acquires from a גוי: אמימר's reading of "לעמיתך", and the ברייתא of the broken vessels with an idol
overview: The amud opens by finishing a derivation: just as a Jew acquires through only one method, a גוי also acquires through only one method, which is money. The גמרא then asks how אמימר, who says משיכה (pulling) works for a גוי, explains the word "לעמיתך". If he follows רבי יוחנן (money acquires by Torah law), the word contrasts money for a Jew with pulling for a גוי. If he follows ריש לקיש (pulling is in the Torah), the word seems extra. The גמרא suggests it teaches that אונאה (overcharging) applies only with a Jew. That is challenged because "אחיו" already excludes a גוי, and answered: one phrase excludes a גוי and the other excludes הקדש, and both are needed. That answer works only if robbing a גוי is forbidden, and anyone who permits it must hold like רבי יוחנן. Then a ברייתא about a Jew who buys broken vessels from a גוי and finds an idol among them challenges the view that money acquires from a גוי. The גמרא first explains it as a case where the גוי accepted Jewish law, and אביי and רבא argue over why the two clauses differ. רב אשי says only money acquires in both clauses. רבינא says pulling acquires in both, and he reads the first clause as a Jew backing out of a verbal deal, which is not a breach of trust (מחוסרי אמנה) with גוים.

steps.title: Just as a Jew acquires with one method, so does a gentile
steps.stepSummary: This closes the previous derivation. A Jew acquires with only one method, and a גוי also acquires with only one method.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as with "your fellow" (a Jew) there is only one way to acquire, so too with a גוי there is only one way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the derivation it was just making. A Jew has only one method of acquiring, so a גוי also has only one method.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse mentions "עמיתך" (your fellow), which shows that a Jew acquires through one specific method. The comparison "מה... אף..." carries this pattern over to a גוי: he also has just one method, but a different one (money, as Sefaria explains). Here a גוי cannot use both methods.

keyTerms.meaning: Your fellow / counterpart, meaning a fellow Jew (from ויקרא כ״ה:י״ד)
"Just as... so too...", a formula for comparing two cases
With one (method of acquisition)

steps.confusionAlert: "באחת" does not mean the Jew and the גוי use the same method. It means each one has only ONE method. A Jew's method is different from a גוי's method.

phrases.english: Just as "your fellow" acquires through one method,
phrases.notes: With a fellow Jew, only one act of acquisition works.

phrases.english: so too a gentile acquires through one method.
phrases.notes: With a gentile, also only one method works (money).

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה ״עֲמִיתֶךָ״ בְּאַחַת, אַף גּוֹי נָמֵי בְּאַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the derivation that came on the previous amud.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A גוי, like a Jew, has only one method of acquisition (money), not two.

steps.title: For אמימר, the verse works well if he agrees with רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what "לעמיתך" teaches according to אמימר, who says משיכה works for a גוי. It first shows that the answer is easy if אמימר follows רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages said: And according to אמימר, who says pulling acquires with a גוי, it works well if he agrees with רבי יוחנן, who says that by Torah law money acquires and pulling does not. Then "לעמיתך" has a purpose: with your fellow by money, with a גוי by pulling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings in אמימר's view and sets up a question. This is the first half of a "הניחא... אלא..." pattern: it explains the side that works out fine before raising the problem in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי יוחנן, Torah law gives a Jew only money as a method of acquisition. So the word "לעמיתך" can teach a contrast: money for a Jew, but pulling for a גוי, which fits אמימר. The word is fully explained on this side.

keyTerms.meaning: "They said": the Sages (or the גמרא) respond
An אמורא who holds that pulling acquires with a gentile
Pulling: a method of acquiring movable objects
"It works out well": the first half of a two-sided challenge
By Torah law, money acquires (רבי יוחנן's view)

phrases.english: They said: And according to Ameimar,
who says pulling acquires with a gentile,
it works out well if he holds
like Rabbi Yoḥanan, who says:

phrases.aramaic: דְּבַר תּוֹרָה מָעוֹת קוֹנוֹת, מְשִׁיכָה לֹא,
phrases.english: by Torah law money acquires, pulling does not,
then "to your fellow" is useful:
with your fellow by money, with a gentile by pulling.
phrases.notes: The word draws a contrast between a Jew and a gentile.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: וּלְאָמֵימָר דְּאָמַר מְשִׁיכָה בְּגוֹי קוֹנָה, הָנִיחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the previous derivation to אמימר's opposing view about a גוי.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does "לעמיתך" teach according to אמימר?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to רבי יוחנן's view, it contrasts money for a Jew with pulling for a גוי.

steps.title: If אמימר agrees with ריש לקיש, the word seems extra
steps.stepSummary: If אמימר follows ריש לקיש, then משיכה works for both a Jew and a גוי, so the word "לעמיתך" has no job.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he agrees with ריש לקיש, who says pulling is written explicitly in the Torah, then with your fellow it is by pulling and with a גוי it is by pulling. So why do I need "לעמיתך"?
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second half of the challenge. Under ריש לקיש's view, the Jew and the גוי are treated the same, so the word "לעמיתך" seems to teach nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש holds that pulling is the Torah's method for a Jew. אמימר says pulling also works for a גוי. Now there is no difference left for "לעמיתך" to point out, so the extra word needs some other explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא, רבי יוחנן's colleague and frequent disputant
Stated explicitly in the Torah
"Why do I need it?": a challenge to a word that seems extra

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִי סָבַר לַהּ כְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ,
phrases.english: But if he holds like Reish Lakish,
who says: pulling is explicit in the Torah,
then with your fellow it is by pulling,
and with a gentile it is by pulling,
so why do I need "to your fellow"?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אִי סָבַר לַהּ כְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the "הניחא... אלא" pattern by raising the problem.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word "לעמיתך" according to אמימר, if he follows ריש לקיש.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If pulling works for both a Jew and a גוי, the word makes no distinction and seems extra.

steps.title: Suggested answer: the word teaches about overcharging
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that "לעמיתך" is not about methods of acquisition. Instead it teaches that אונאה is returned to a Jew but not to a גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: To your fellow you return overcharging, but you do not return overcharging to a גוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to give "לעמיתך" a new job. It connects the word to the rule of אונאה later in the same verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse goes on to say "אל תונו איש את אחיו". The suggestion is that "לעמיתך" limits the duty to return an overcharge to dealings with a fellow Jew. This would make the word useful even under ריש לקיש.

keyTerms.meaning: Overcharging or underpaying beyond the accepted margin in a sale
Returns (the overcharged amount)

phrases.english: They said: to your fellow you return overcharging,
but you do not return overcharging to a gentile.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of why "לעמיתך" is needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the extra word a different purpose (אונאה instead of methods of acquisition).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word "לעמיתך" seemed extra under ריש לקיש's view.
steps.terutzMaskana: It would teach that אונאה is returned only to a Jew.

steps.title: Rejected: that rule already comes from "his brother"
steps.stepSummary: The answer is rejected. The exemption from returning אונאה to a גוי is already learned from "אל תונו איש את אחיו", so "לעמיתך" is still extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: The rule for a גוי comes from "A man shall not overcharge his brother"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the answer from the previous step. Another part of the verse already teaches the rule about a גוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words "אחיו" (his brother) already leave out a גוי from the rule of אונאה. So "לעמיתך" cannot be needed for that rule, and the question from step 3 comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: "A man shall not overcharge his brother" (ויקרא כ״ה:י״ד)
"It is derived / comes out from"

steps.whatToRemember: At this point the אונאה answer seems to fail, because "אחיו" already excludes a גוי. The next step rescues it: one phrase excludes a גוי and the other excludes הקדש.

phrases.english: For a gentile, that is derived from "Do not overcharge
a man his brother"!
phrases.notes: "His brother" already leaves out a gentile.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְגוֹי — מֵ״אַל תּוֹנוּ אִישׁ אֶת אָחִיו״ נָפְקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer given in step 4.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using "לעמיתך" to teach the אונאה rule.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The word would be repeating a rule that "אחיו" already teaches.

steps.title: One phrase excludes a gentile and one excludes consecrated property
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the problem from Step 5. The Torah's two phrases about אונאה are not repeating each other. One teaches that there is no אונאה with a גוי, and the other teaches that there is no אונאה with הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: One phrase is for a gentile, and one is for consecrated property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the reading from Step 4. It shows that each of the two phrases has its own job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 said the exclusion of a גוי was already learned from "אל תונו איש את אחיו", so the other phrase looked extra. The answer splits the work. One phrase excludes a גוי, and the other excludes הקדש. Now neither phrase is extra.

keyTerms.meaning: Overcharging or underpaying beyond the fair price in a sale
Property consecrated to the בית המקדש
A non-Jew

phrases.english: One is for a gentile,
phrases.notes: One phrase teaches that there is no אונאה with a גוי.

phrases.english: and one is for consecrated property.
phrases.notes: The other phrase teaches that there is no אונאה with הקדש.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the rejection in Step 5 by giving each phrase its own job.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the derivations: two phrases teach two different exclusions
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both phrases seemed to exclude only a גוי, so one of them was extra.
steps.terutzMaskana: One phrase excludes a גוי and the other excludes הקדש.

steps.title: Why both exclusions are needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why the Torah could not write just one exclusion. If only one were written, we would think only a גוי is excluded and that הקדש still has אונאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both are needed. If the Torah had written only one, I would have said that only a gentile has no אונאה, but consecrated property does. So the Torah teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the two exclusions cannot be learned from each other, so both phrases are needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a צריכותא, a proof that both teachings are necessary. A גוי is outside the מצוה of fairness between Jews, but הקדש belongs to Heaven, so we might have thought it gets more protection. The second phrase teaches that הקדש also has no אונאה.

keyTerms.meaning: And they are necessary. This opens a proof that both sources are needed.
I would have thought (a mistaken first assumption)
It teaches us (the verse corrects the mistake)

phrases.english: And both are necessary,
for if the Merciful One had written only one,
I would have said:
it is a gentile who has no exploitation,
but consecrated property does have exploitation;
so it teaches us otherwise.
phrases.notes: The second phrase teaches that הקדש also has no אונאה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports Step 6 by showing that neither exclusion could be learned from the other.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: proving that both teachings are needed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With only one phrase, we would exclude only a גוי, and הקדש would still have אונאה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both phrases are needed. A גוי and הקדש are each excluded from אונאה.

steps.title: If robbing a gentile is permitted, why would a verse be needed for overcharging?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges Step 6. The answer only works for someone who says robbing a גוי is forbidden. For someone who says it is permitted, overcharging a גוי would obviously be allowed, so no verse is needed for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for the one who says robbing a gentile is forbidden. That is why a verse is needed to permit overcharging. But if אמימר holds like the one who says robbing a gentile is permitted, do we need a verse to permit overcharging?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer of Step 6 from a new direction. Under one view about robbing a גוי, the phrase excluding a גוי would again have no job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If even outright גזל from a גוי is allowed, then the smaller thing, אונאה, is surely allowed too, and no verse is needed. That would leave one phrase extra again. So the question is which view אמימר holds.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well (for one view, but what about the other?)
Robbing him (here, robbing a גוי)
Is it needed? (The point is that it is obvious.)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a debate about whether robbing a גוי is permitted. The גמרא only asks how the verse would be explained by each existing view.

phrases.english: This works well according to the one who says his robbery is forbidden;
that is why a verse is needed to permit exploitation.
But if he holds

phrases.aramaic: כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר גְּזֵילוֹ שֶׁל גּוֹי מוּתָּר,
phrases.english: like the one who says robbing a gentile is permitted,
is a verse needed for exploitation?
phrases.notes: If robbery is permitted, overcharging is surely permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 6 by showing that its answer depends on the view about robbing a גוי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 6 that a verse is needed to exclude a גוי from אונאה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If robbing a גוי is permitted, overcharging him is obviously permitted, so the verse is extra again.

steps.title: Such a person must hold like רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that if אמימר holds robbing a גוי is permitted, he must hold like רבי יוחנן. Then "לעמיתך" is explained the easy way from Step 2, as teaching about methods of acquisition.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: if he holds like the one who says robbing a gentile is permitted, then he must hold like רבי יוחנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the challenge by linking the two views. Whoever permits robbing a גוי must follow רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי יוחנן, money acquires by Torah law. So "לעמיתך" can teach that a Jew acquires with money and a גוי with משיכה, which Step 2 already called easy. The אונאה explanation is only needed by someone who holds robbing a גוי is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: They said (an answer given by the Sages)
You have no choice but to say; necessarily

steps.whatToRemember: For אמימר: if he follows רבי יוחנן, "לעמיתך" teaches about methods of acquisition (money for a Jew, pulling for a גוי). If he follows ריש לקיש, the word teaches about אונאה. That works only if robbing a גוי is forbidden. Anyone who permits robbing a גוי must follow רבי יוחנן.

phrases.english: They said:

phrases.aramaic: אִי סָבַר לַהּ כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר גְּזֵילוֹ מוּתָּר —
phrases.english: if he holds like the one who says his robbery is permitted,

phrases.aramaic: עַל כּוּרְחָיךְ כְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן סְבִירָא לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: then by necessity he holds like רבי יוחנן.
phrases.notes: רבי יוחנן holds that money acquires by Torah law, so the explanation from Step 2 works.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: אִי סָבַר לַהּ כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר גְּזֵילוֹ מוּתָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 8 by sending that view back to the easy explanation in Step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Linking views: one position forces the other
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Someone who permits robbing a גוי would have no use for the verse.
steps.terutzMaskana: Such a person follows רבי יוחנן, so the verse teaches about methods of acquisition.

steps.title: A ברייתא about buying broken vessels with an idol inside
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא. A Jew buys broken vessels from a גוי and finds an idol among them. If he pulled them before paying, he returns the idol. If he pulled them after paying, he must throw it into the Dead Sea. The גמרא asks why pulling matters if money acquires from a גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection. One who buys broken vessels from gentiles and finds an idol among them: if he pulled them before he gave the money, he returns it. If he pulled them after he gave the money, he takes it to the Dead Sea. And if you say money acquires, why do I need pulling?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new challenge from a ברייתא against the view that a Jew acquires from a גוי with money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, ownership seems to depend on whether the payment came before or after the pulling. Either way, the pulling is what counts. If money alone acquired from a גוי, the Jew would own the vessels as soon as he paid, and pulling would not matter.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection (from an earlier source)
Broken pieces of metal vessels
Idol worship; an idol
Pulling the item, a formal way of acquiring it
The Dead Sea, where forbidden items are thrown so no one can benefit from them

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
one who buys broken vessels from the gentiles
and finds an idol among them:

phrases.aramaic: אִם עַד שֶׁלֹּא נָתַן מָעוֹת מָשַׁךְ —
phrases.english: if he pulled them before he gave the money,
he returns it;
phrases.notes: He did not yet own it, so he may give it back.

phrases.english: and if he pulled them after he gave the money,
he must take the benefit to the Dead Sea.
phrases.notes: He owns the idol, so he must get rid of it.

phrases.english: And if you say money acquires,
why do I need pulling?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new challenge, now against the view that money acquires from a גוי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that a Jew acquires from a גוי by paying money
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא makes ownership depend on pulling, so money alone must not acquire from a גוי.

steps.title: The gentile agreed to follow Jewish law
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is about a גוי who agreed to have the deal judged by Jewish law. In that case the Jewish rule of acquiring through משיכה applies.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here we are dealing with a case where the gentile accepted upon himself to be judged by Jewish law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits the ברייתא to a special case, so it no longer contradicts the view that money acquires from a גוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally money acquires from a גוי. Here the גוי chose Jewish law, under which movable items are acquired with משיכה. That is why pulling matters in this ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, what case are we dealing with? (This limits a source to a specific case.)
Jewish law

phrases.english: Here, what case are we dealing with?
One where he accepted upon himself to be judged by Jewish law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 10 by limiting the ברייתא to a special case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא shows that a Jew always needs pulling to acquire from a גוי.
steps.terutzMaskana: Pulling is needed only because this גוי accepted Jewish law.

steps.title: Then why mention money at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer in Step 11. If Jewish law applies, pulling alone acquires, so why does the ברייתא mention whether the money was given?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why do I need money?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on Step 11. Under Jewish law, the mention of money in the ברייתא looks unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under Jewish law, משיכה acquires by itself, so payment should make no difference. Yet the ברייתא divides its cases by whether money was given before or after the pulling. That seems to show money plays some role.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if your answer is true)

phrases.english: If so, why do I need money?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in Step 11 using the wording of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 11 that Jewish law applies
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If only משיכה matters under Jewish law, then mentioning money in the ברייתא serves no purpose.

steps.title: Even after paying, only pulling counts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the ברייתא's point. Even though the Jew paid, everything still depends on pulling. If he pulled, he acquired. If not, he did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: even though he gave money, if he pulled, yes, he acquired, and if not, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא. Money is mentioned to teach that paying does not acquire, and only pulling does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mention of money is not there because money helps acquire. It is there to show that even after paying, the deal is not done without משיכה. This fits the case of a גוי who accepted Jewish law.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means (rereading the source)
Even though

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא about broken vessels is about a גוי who accepted Jewish law. There, only משיכה acquires, even after money was paid. So it does not disprove that money acquires from a גוי in an ordinary case.

phrases.english: This is what it means:
even though he gave money,
if he pulled, yes, he acquired;
and if not, no, he did not acquire.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנָּתַן מָעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 12 by rereading why the ברייתא mentions money.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא mentions money because money helps acquire.
steps.terutzMaskana: Money is mentioned to show that even after payment, only pulling acquires.

steps.title: If pulling acquires, the first clause is a problem
steps.stepSummary: If משיכה acquires, then in the first clause the Jew already acquired the idol by pulling it. So why may he return it?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the first clause is difficult!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer of Step 13 from the other half of the ברייתא. If pulling acquires, the first clause makes no sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 13 said that under Jewish law, pulling alone acquires. But the first clause says that if he pulled before paying, he gives the idol back to the גוי. If pulling acquired, the idol would already be his, and he should have to destroy it, not return it.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: if what you just said is true
It is difficult; there is a problem
The first clause (the 'head') of a teaching

phrases.english: If so, the first clause is difficult!
phrases.notes: The first clause: he pulled before paying, so he returns the idol. If pulling acquires, why return it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 13 using the first clause of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 13 that the ברייתא follows Jewish law, where משיכה acquires.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If pulling acquires, the Jew in the first clause already owns the idol, so returning it to the גוי should not be allowed.

steps.title: אביי: the first clause is a mistaken deal
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that in the first clause the deal is cancelled as a מקח טעות, so the Jew never truly acquired the idol.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: the first clause rules this way because there is a mistaken transaction.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question from Step 14. Pulling does acquire, but here the sale was a mistake, so it falls apart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Jew meant to buy broken vessels, not an idol. A sale made under a mistake is cancelled, so the idol never became his. Since it is not his, he may simply return it.

keyTerms.meaning: A mistaken transaction. A sale that is void because the buyer did not knowingly agree to what he got
אביי, an אמורא from Babylonia

phrases.english: Abaye said:
The first clause is because there is a mistaken transaction.
phrases.notes: He never wanted to buy an idol, so the sale is void.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: רֵישָׁא מִשּׁוּם דְּאִיכָּא מִקָּח טָעוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the acquisition is cancelled because of a mistake.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Pulling acquired the idol, so returning it should be forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: The pulling would have acquired, but the sale is void as a מקח טעות, so the idol goes back.

steps.title: רבא: the second clause is also a mistake
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges אביי. The Jew did not want the idol in the second clause either, so that should also be a מקח טעות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: the first clause is because there is a mistaken transaction, and in the second clause there is no mistaken transaction?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks אביי's answer. Your reason for the first clause should apply to the second clause too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both clauses the Jew bought broken vessels and found an idol he never wanted. If the mistake cancels the first sale, it should cancel the second one too. Then why must he throw the idol into the Dead Sea in the second clause instead of returning it?

keyTerms.meaning: The last clause (the 'end') of a teaching
רבא, an אמורא, a frequent partner of אביי in debate

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
The first clause is because there is a mistaken transaction,
in the second clause there is no mistaken transaction?
phrases.notes: A rhetorical question: surely it is also a mistake there.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: רֵישָׁא מִשּׁוּם דְּאִיכָּא מִקָּח טָעוּת, סֵיפָא לֵיכָּא מִקָּח טָעוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי's answer in Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's claim that the first clause is a מקח טעות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The mistake is the same in both clauses, so the reason cannot explain why the two clauses have different rulings.

steps.title: רבא: both are mistakes, but paying makes it look like the Jew owns the idol
steps.stepSummary: רבא says both clauses are a מקח טעות. The difference is appearance: before paying, it does not look like the Jew owns an idol. After paying, it does.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: the first and second clauses are both mistaken transactions. In the first clause, where he did not pay money, it does not look like an idol in the hand of a Jew. In the second clause, where he paid money, it looks like an idol in the hand of a Jew.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his own answer in place of אביי's. Both sales are mistakes, and the different rulings come from how things look.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In neither clause does the Jew truly acquire the idol. But once he has paid, people see the deal as finished, and it looks as if a Jew owned an idol. Because of that look, he may not return it and must destroy it. Before paying, it does not look that way, so he may give it back.

keyTerms.meaning: It appears; it looks like (to onlookers)
Money; coins (literally זוזים)
Idol worship; an idol

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
The first clause and the second clause are both a mistaken transaction,
in the first clause, where he did not give money,

phrases.aramaic: לָא מִיחְזֵי כַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה בְּיַד יִשְׂרָאֵל,
phrases.english: it does not look like an idol in the possession of a Jew,
phrases.notes: So he may return it.

phrases.english: in the second clause, where he gave money,
it looks like an idol in the possession of a Jew.
phrases.notes: So he must destroy it, not return it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: רֵישָׁא וְסֵיפָא מִקָּח טָעוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting אביי's answer in Step 16, רבא offers his own answer to Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction based on appearance (how it looks to others), not on legal ownership.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only the first clause is a mistaken sale, which leaves no reason for the second clause to be different.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both sales are void, but once money was paid it looks like a Jew owns an idol, so it must be destroyed.
steps.confusionAlert: For רבא, the Jew does not legally own the idol in the second clause either. He must destroy it only because of how it looks once he has paid.

steps.title: אביי's defense: after paying, he should have checked
steps.stepSummary: אביי can answer רבא. In the first clause the buyer had not paid, so he had not inspected yet, and it is a true mistake. In the second clause he had paid, so he should have inspected before pulling. His failure to check means the sale stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: And אביי could say to you: the first clause is a mistaken transaction, because he did not know, since he had not yet given him money. The second clause is not a mistaken transaction, because once he gave money, when he pulled he should have inspected and only then pulled.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends אביי against רבא's challenge in Step 16. It explains why only the first clause counts as a mistake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before paying, a buyer has not yet committed to the deal and has no reason to inspect, so his not knowing is a real mistake. Once he has paid, he is expected to check what he takes. If he pulls without checking, he accepted whatever was there, so the sale is valid. The idol is then truly his, and he must destroy it.

keyTerms.meaning: To inspect; to examine carefully
He should have (done something)
Since; once

phrases.english: And Abaye could say to you:
The first clause is a mistaken transaction, because he did not know,
since he had not given him the money.
phrases.notes: Before paying, he had no reason to inspect yet.

phrases.english: The second clause is not a mistaken transaction,
because once he gave the money,
when he was pulling,
he should have inspected and then pulled.
phrases.notes: He did not check, so he accepted what he took, and the sale stands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to אביי's answer (Step 15) and defends it against רבא's challenge (Step 16).
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the two cases: a buyer who has paid carries a duty to inspect.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The mistake is the same in both clauses, as רבא argued.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only before paying is not knowing a real mistake. After paying, failing to inspect means he accepted the sale.
steps.whyThisMatters: אביי and רבא now disagree on why the second clause requires destroying the idol. For אביי the Jew truly owns it. For רבא it only looks that way.

steps.title: רב אשי: pulling never acquires here, and 'pulled' is just matching wording
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains that the ברייתא follows the גוי's rules, where only money acquires. Pulling does nothing in either clause. The second clause says 'pulled' only to match the wording of the first clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: from the first clause we see that pulling does not acquire, so in the second clause too pulling does not acquire. Since the first clause taught 'pulled,' the second clause also taught 'pulled.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a completely different answer to the original question from Step 10 (why does pulling matter if money acquires from a גוי?). He says pulling does not matter at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first clause proves that pulling alone does not acquire, since he returns the idol. So in the second clause it is the money that acquired, not the pulling. The word 'pulled' appears in the second clause only because the ברייתא used that word in the first clause, so it kept the same style.

keyTerms.meaning: רב אשי, a late אמורא, the main editor of the תלמוד בבלי
Pulling does not acquire
Since it taught; a word repeated only to match the earlier wording

steps.whatToRemember: So far there are three approaches to the ברייתא. אביי: pulling acquires; the first clause is a mistaken sale, but after paying he should have checked. רבא: both are mistaken sales; after paying it only looks like the Jew owns the idol. רב אשי: the gentile rule applies, so only money acquires, and 'pulled' in the second clause is just matching wording. The next step brings a fourth approach, from רבינא.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רב אשי holds that pulling matters in the second clause. He says the word 'pulled' there carries no legal meaning at all.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Since in the first clause pulling does not acquire,
in the second clause too pulling does not acquire,
phrases.notes: It is the money that acquires, under the rules for a גוי.

phrases.english: and since the first clause taught 'pulled,'
the second clause also taught 'pulled.'
phrases.notes: The word is there only for matching style.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: מִדְּרֵישָׁא מְשִׁיכָה אֵינָהּ קוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אביי and רבא line (based on Step 11) and answers the original קשיא of Step 10 differently.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Wording explanation: the word is repeated for matching style (איידי).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word 'pulled' in the second clause shows that pulling is needed to acquire.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only money acquires from a גוי. The word 'pulled' in the second clause is just there to match the first clause.
steps.whyThisMatters: This saves the view that money acquires from a גוי without needing the special case of Step 11, where the גוי agreed to Jewish law.

steps.title: רבינא: Pulling acquires in both clauses
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says the second clause proves that משיכה acquires, so it must acquire in the first clause too. He rereads the first clause as a case where the Jew neither paid nor pulled.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: Since in the second clause pulling acquires, in the first clause too pulling acquires. The first clause is really saying this: if he did not pay and did not pull, he may go back.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא offers a fourth way to settle the contradiction between the two clauses of the ברייתא. He keeps one rule for both clauses (pulling acquires) by changing how we read the first clause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי said both clauses follow the גוי's rules, where only money acquires. רבינא goes the other way: both clauses follow the Jewish rule, where משיכה acquires (the deal was set up under Jewish law). The first clause no longer describes someone who pulled. It describes someone who did nothing yet, so nothing was acquired and he can still pull out.

keyTerms.meaning: Pulling: a physical act of acquisition in which the buyer draws the item toward himself
Acquires, makes the purchase legally binding
The first clause of a teaching
The latter (second) clause of a teaching
'This is what it is saying'. Introduces a reinterpretation of a text

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבינא is adding words to the ברייתא at random. He is fixing the first clause so that it matches the rule (pulling acquires) which the second clause already shows.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
From the fact that in the latter clause pulling acquires,
in the first clause too, pulling acquires,
phrases.notes: The deal is understood as following Jewish law.

phrases.english: and the first clause is saying this:

phrases.aramaic: אִם לֹא נָתַן וְלֹא מָשַׁךְ — יַחְזוֹר.
phrases.english: if he did not give the money and did not pull, he may go back.
phrases.notes: This rereads the first clause. Nothing at all was done to acquire.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an approach opposite to רב אשי's. רב אשי said only money acquires in both clauses; רבינא says pulling acquires in both (the deal follows Jewish law, as in Step 11), and answers the problem of the first clause from Step 14 by rereading it.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the first clause (הכי קאמר)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first clause seemed to say the Jew pulled the item and could still return it, which clashes with the second clause, where pulling acquires.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both clauses agree that pulling acquires. The first clause speaks of a Jew who neither paid nor pulled, so he may back out.

steps.title: What does 'go back' mean here?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'יחזור' means, since in רבינא's reading nothing was handed over that needs returning.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'he may go back' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short clarifying question about the word 'יחזור'. This sets up the next step, which gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the old reading, 'יחזור' meant returning the item the Jew had pulled. In רבינא's reading the Jew never pulled or paid, so there is nothing physical to return. The word needs a new meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: What? Introduces a question of definition
He goes back / returns

phrases.english: What does 'he may go back' mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies a word in רבינא's new reading of the first clause.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What 'going back' means when no item was taken and no money was paid.

steps.title: He backs out of his words
steps.stepSummary: 'יחזור' means the Jew may back out of his verbal agreement to buy.
steps.simpleTranslation: He goes back on his words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: 'going back' means the Jew may cancel what he had only agreed to verbally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Jew had promised with words to buy, but he never did a binding act (paying or pulling). So the ברייתא is telling us he does not have to finish the purchase.

keyTerms.meaning: Words: a verbal agreement with no act of acquisition

phrases.english: He goes back on his words.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'יחזור' means backing out of a verbal commitment to buy.

steps.title: Why the ברייתא had to say this
steps.stepSummary: The תנא holds that backing out of a verbal deal is a breach of trust (מחוסרי אמנה). That applies only between Jews, who keep their word, and not in a deal with גוים, who do not. So the ברייתא needed to teach that the Jew may freely back out here.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds that words carry the issue of 'lacking trustworthiness'. But this applies only to a Jew buying from a Jew, since Jews stand by their words. A Jew buying from gentiles, who do not stand by their words, is not included.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the ברייתא needed to teach something that sounds obvious: that someone who has done nothing binding can back out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This תנא holds that backing out of a verbal deal is normally improper and counts as מחוסרי אמנה (lacking trustworthiness), so we might have thought the Jew must keep his word. The ברייתא teaches that this concern exists only between Jews, who rely on each other's words. In a deal with גוים, neither side relies on mere words, so backing out is no breach of trust.

keyTerms.meaning: He (the תנא) holds
Lacking trustworthiness: improper conduct by someone who breaks his word
'And these words apply only…'. Limits the scope of a rule
They stand by their spoken words

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבינא, both clauses follow the rule that משיכה acquires. The first clause speaks of a Jew who only agreed verbally. He may back out, because the breach of trust called מחוסרי אמנה applies only in deals between Jews.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches an important general principle: backing out of a purely verbal deal is legally allowed but morally frowned upon (מחוסרי אמנה). The concern depends on whether both sides normally rely on each other's word.

phrases.english: He holds: words carry
the issue of lacking trustworthiness,
phrases.notes: Backing out of a verbal deal is improper conduct.

phrases.english: but this applies only to a Jew buying from a Jew,
since they stand by their words,
but a Jew buying from gentiles,
since they do not stand by their words, no.
phrases.notes: Neither side relies on the other's word, so backing out is not a breach of trust.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָסָבַר: דְּבָרִים יֵשׁ בָּהֶם מִשּׁוּם מְחוּסְּרֵי אֲמָנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the ruling of step 22 needed to be taught, which answers an unstated question.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why a seemingly obvious ruling needed to be taught
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since backing out of words is מחוסרי אמנה, one might think the Jew must complete the purchase.
steps.terutzMaskana: מחוסרי אמנה applies only between Jews. With גוים, the Jew may freely back out.
